title: The present perfect: he hablado
topic: pretérito perfecto; regular participles; hoy, esta semana, ya, todavía no, alguna vez
why: The first past tense of the course: after the present, ir a + infinitive and estar + gerund, you discover the pretérito perfecto, built like the English present perfect. The lesson focuses on what differs from English (always haber, never anything between haber and the participle, used in Spain for anything that happened today or this week) and prepares the contrast with the indefinido in the next lesson.

He hablado: haber + participle

Good news: the pretérito perfecto is built just like the English present perfect (“I have spoken”), with an auxiliary in the present followed by a past participle. The auxiliary is haber, a verb used almost only for this (“to have” in the sense of owning is always tener).

hablarcomervivir
yohe habladohe comidohe vivido
túhas habladohas comidohas vivido
él, ella, ustedha habladoha comidoha vivido
nosotros, nosotrashemos habladohemos comidohemos vivido
vosotros, vosotrashabéis habladohabéis comidohabéis vivido
ellos, ellas, ustedeshan habladohan comidohan vivido

The participle: -ado or -ido

-ar verbs take -ado: trabajar → trabajado, llegar → llegado. -er and -ir verbs take -ido: comer → comido, salir → salido. Even verbs that are irregular in the present often have a regular participle: ir → ido, ser → sido, estar → estado, tener → tenido, poder → podido, querer → querido.

Three things to watch

  • Always haber, never tener, even though English uses “have” for both: he ido (I've gone), ha llegado (he has arrived), me he levantado (I've gotten up).
  • The participle never changes, just like in English: Marta ha llegado, las chicas han salido, la he llamado (I've called her).
  • Never separate haber from the participle. English says “I have already eaten”, “I have not seen”; in Spanish, pronouns and no go in front of haber, and nothing goes in between.
No lo he comprado. Me he duchado.I haven't bought it. I've taken a shower.

“I've gotten up” = me he levantado: the pronoun, then he, then the participle in -o, whether you're a man or a woman. Never “he me levantado”.

", "

A past that still touches today

The perfecto is used for a past connected to the present, a bit like the English present perfect: an action done in a period that isn't over yet (today, this week, this year), or a life experience with no specific date. But Spain, and especially Madrid, goes further than English: it uses it for anything that happened today, even with a precise time like “this morning”, where English switches to the past simple. For “yesterday” or “last year”, Spanish uses another tense, the indefinido, which you'll see in the next lesson.

Time markerExampleTranslation
hoyHoy he trabajado en casa.I've worked from home today.
esta mañanaEsta mañana he desayunado con Pablo.This morning I had breakfast with Pablo.
esta semanaEsta semana hemos comido fuera tres veces.This week we've eaten out three times.
este añoEste año he viajado mucho.This year I've traveled a lot.
yaYa he terminado.I've already finished.
todavía noTodavía no he comido.I haven't eaten yet.
nuncaNunca he estado en Cádiz.I've never been to Cádiz.
alguna vez¿Has probado alguna vez el pulpo?Have you ever tried octopus?

Ya or alguna vez: “already” or “ever”

English separates these two ideas, and so does Spanish. Ya means it's done: Ya he comido (I've already eaten, no need to do it anymore). Alguna vez asks whether it has happened at least once in your life: ¿Has estado alguna vez en Sevilla? You answer with nunca, una vez, dos veces, muchas veces.

¿Has comido ya? — No, todavía no.Have you eaten yet? — No, not yet.
¿Has estado alguna vez en Sevilla? — Sí, dos veces.Have you ever been to Seville? — Yes, twice.

Nunca at the beginning of a sentence is used without no: Nunca he estado en Cádiz. Placed after the verb, it needs no in front: No he estado nunca en Cádiz. Yes, a double negative: in Spanish it's correct.

In Latin America, and in a few regions of Spain (Galicia, Asturias, the Canary Islands), the perfecto is used much less. This course follows the usage of Madrid.

", "

Eight irregular participles

The vast majority of participles are regular. Here are the eight most common irregular ones: learn them by heart, because they come up all the time. Just like English “done”, “said” or “written”, they don't follow the rule (dicho / said, escrito / written).

InfinitiveParticipleExampleTranslation
hacerhecho¿Qué has hecho hoy?What have you done today?
decirdicho¿Qué ha dicho Marta?What did Marta say?
vervistoEsta semana he visto dos películas.This week I've seen two movies.
escribirescritoYa he escrito el correo.I've already written the email.
volvervueltoMis padres todavía no han vuelto.My parents haven't come back yet.
ponerpuesto¿Dónde has puesto las llaves?Where have you put the keys?
abrirabiertoHoy han abierto un bar nuevo.A new bar opened today.
romperrotoLos niños han roto un vaso.The kids have broken a glass.

Hecho is spelled with an h: it's the participle of hacer. And when the ending -ido follows an a, an e or an o, it takes a written accent: leer → leído, oír → oído.

All together

Hoy me he levantado temprano, he escrito tres correos y he vuelto a casa a las seis.Today I got up early, wrote three emails and came back home at six.
¿Has visto a Javier esta semana? — No, todavía no lo he visto.Have you seen Javier this week? — No, I haven't seen him yet.

Notice the a in front of Javier: it's the “personal a” you already know (he visto a Javier, but he visto la película). And the pronoun lo always goes in front of haber.
